strengths: Slides 3–5 use purpose-built diagrams rather than stock decoration: expanding marker distances, a three-stage cooling sequence, and stretched wavelengths.
Slide 7 responsibly separates the model's evidence-supported history from unanswered origin questions.
Slide 8 closes with a concise expansion/cooling/evidence recap and directly answers the likely misconception about a single cosmic location.
The dark navy, cyan, white, and muted-gold palette is consistent, with generally strong contrast.

issues.evidence: Generation defect: the caption beneath the right diagram is visibly cut off at the frame edge as "NO PRIVILEGED CENTER / NO OUTER S..."; this matches the reported overflow.
issues.fix: Shorten or wrap the caption and constrain the full diagram group inside the safe area. This must be corrected before the deck is ready.

issues.evidence: Selection/design defect: slides 2, 4, 7, and 8 largely resemble a sober corporate science template. Pirate specificity is carried mostly by words such as "log," "chart," and "bearings," rather than by an illustrated voyage system.
issues.fix: Carry a coherent navigator-chart visual language through the explanatory slides, using illustrated instruments, map conventions, and voyage progress without replacing the scientific diagrams.

issues.evidence: The concentric-ring composition places "Observer Now" at the visual center. Although the text denies a central blast point, the diagram can inadvertently suggest that the observer occupies a privileged cosmic center, and the surrounding boxes do not clearly depict an all-sky microwave signal.
issues.fix: Use an all-sky projection or a multiple-observer diagram showing that observers in different locations receive background radiation from every direction.

issues.evidence: The sequence is readable, but "Early" and "Later" are too vague beside the precise 380,000-year marker, and the equal spacing could be mistaken for elapsed-time scale.
issues.fix: Label the timeline as schematic and add approximate timing for nuclei and later structure formation.

A.signatureMoment: Slide 5 is the strongest substantive moment: the two wavelength traces make cosmological redshift immediately visible, while the nautical "wake" language remains secondary to the science.

strengths: Slide 1 is a memorable, brief-specific opening: the illustrated brass telescope, celestial chart, tiny ship, and "three bearings" framing immediately establish a polished cosmic voyage.
Slide 3 clearly shows the same three labeled markers separating when the grid enlarges; the paired frames communicate expansion more effectively than prose alone.
Slide 5 uses well-separated waveform panels, color, and crest spacing to make longer wavelength legible at projection size.
Slides 2 and 6 sustain the illustrated star-chart and instrument motif rather than abandoning it after the cover.
Slides 7–8 provide a disciplined ending: uncertainty is explicitly bounded before the three-part synthesis and direct answer.
All eight slides appear unclipped, use strong contrast, and maintain a coherent navy, cream, cyan, brass, and coral palette.

issues.evidence: The telescope and enormous textured celestial globe are atmospheric rather than explanatory; they do not show the actual all-sky pattern of the cosmic microwave background and could be read as a literal object overhead.
issues.fix: Replace or overlay the globe with a clearly labeled stylized all-sky CMB map, while retaining the telescope as the pirate-facing frame.

issues.evidence: The approximate 380,000-year milestone is presented without a visible source on this slide, unlike the sourced 13.8-billion-year and redshift claims elsewhere.
issues.fix: Add a compact NASA or ESA source footer and identify the timeline as schematic rather than proportional.

issues.evidence: The generated right-side image contains chart-like rings, grids, and markings without a legend. It is visually effective but could be mistaken for scientific evidence rather than concept illustration.
issues.fix: Label it as an illustrative star chart or simplify the pseudo-technical markings.

B.signatureMoment: Slide 5's paired short- and long-wavelength panels are the best union of pirate-voyage language and useful science visualization.

result.reason: B is the deck to give the user. It passes the slide-count, palette, subject-coverage, readability, and clipping checks, while A is blocked from readiness by the visible slide 3 overflow. B also realizes the requested pirate space-voyage premise across the full deck rather than relying mainly on nautical wording. The preference is not dependent on which deck is inspected first: B has repeated advantages on slides 1, 3, 5, 6, and 8. A's most valuable improvement would be to rebuild its largely corporate middle in the same audience-specific illustrated navigator system while preserving its sound science diagrams. Route identity is unavailable, so an "original arm" cannot be identified; judged only from the renders, B's greater visual complexity earns its keep through stronger audience fit and clearer continuity. B exceeds competent default quality, but its strongest illustrations remain partly atmospheric, so it does not earn sustained wow.
result.whatWouldMakeWinnerExceptional: Create one exceptional, evidence-bearing voyage map that persists across the deck and spatially connects expansion, cooling, redshift, and the all-sky CMB. Replacing slide 6's decorative globe with an accurate stylized CMB projection and adding sourced time markers would turn the attractive theme into a genuinely distinctive explanatory system.
